text: Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Lauren Chernov, and I am calling this Specialized Programs and Centers Committee meeting on August 6, 2026, to order. I am joined by my colleague, Ms. Donahue, and Mr. Pepper is out today, so it's just the two of us. Welcome, and we are glad you are here. We do not have any public comment today, so we will move on to item number three, which is approval of the draft minutes from June 3rd, 2026, meeting. Ms.

Donahue, do you have any additions or corrections? Thank you, Chair Chernov. I was not present for the last meeting, but having reviewed the recording of the previous meeting, I'm satisfied with the draft minutes and that they adequately represent what transpired at that meeting, and I do not have any changes. With that, I will make a motion to approve the draft minutes for the June 3rd, 2026, Specialized Programs and Centers Committee meeting. Second. I have a second. All those in favor? Aye.

None opposed. That passes unanimously to zer-- Well, not unanimously. Two to zero with one absent, one not present, Mr. Pepper. All right. We will now move on to our information items. We have two very exciting presentations today. To kick us off, to get us back into the groove, today we will start with 4.01, Family and Community Engagement, the FACE Office Resource Hub. And presenting today is Ms. Renee Dawson, the director of Family and Community

Engagement. She is joined by Ms. Danielle Nadler, the executive director of Loudoun Education Foundation, and Ms. Sarah Boyce, our supervisor of outreach services, all from our Family and Community Engagement office. So we are so glad to have you. The floor is yours. So good afternoon. I'm Renee Dawson, director of Family and Community Engagement, and, as was shared, I'm joined by two esteemed guests, Danielle Nadler

and Sarah Boyce. We are presenting a collaborative vision for the LCPS FACE Resource Hub. This initiative builds on the work already happening across LCPS and the Loudoun Education Foundation to create a more coordinated and accessible system of support for students and families.

So what is this FACE Resource Hub? The FACE Resource Hub would serve as a centralized referral-based system designed to respond to emerging needs that may create barriers to student learning. Through school-based referrals, the hub would help ensure students and families can access essential resources with dignity, consistency, and care. The model brings together complementary supports with LEF Fueled continuing its

established work to address food insecurity while the FACE Resource Hub coordinates access to clothing, hygiene items, school supplies, and other essential resources. Together, these efforts would help schools respond to immediate needs so that our students can remain focused, engaged, and ready to learn. So why? Well, students cannot fully engage in learning when essential needs create

barriers to their success. Research has consistently shown that when schools work alongside with families and community partners to reduce those barriers, students are better positioned to attend school consistently, engage in learning, and achieve stronger outcomes. One of Loudoun County's greatest strengths is its extraordinary spirit of generosity, and each year, community and business partners

donate thousands of items to support LCPS students and families. The FACE Resource Hub would create an infrastructure to connect that generosity more intentionally and identified student needs with identified student needs across our division. Rather than individual schools independently locating, storing, and distributing our resources, the hub would provide a coordinated

system for receiving and inventorying and distributing donations based on school referrals and documented needs. For example, okay, if a community partner donates 1,000 backpacks, the hub could identify where those backpacks are most needed and coordinate their distribution across the schools, and this approach would help resources reach the

students who need them while also making it easier for our community partners to give in meaningful and impactful ways. So how would we do this? The FACE Resource Hub would operate through a consistent school-based referral process, and when an emerging student need is identified, dedicated school staff would submit a referral to the hub. The hub staff would review the request, coordinate those resources, fulfill that

need, and support distribution back to the school. This closed-loop process allows us to track requests, to inventory, and to fulfill the recurring needs while helping ensure that resources are distributed efficiently and equitably and with accountability. And the great part of this is the co-location with LEF would allow both programs to

leverage that shared infrastructure, strengthen coordination, and maximize available resources while maintaining our distinct programs and operations. And importantly, the FACE Resource Hub is designed to coordinate and strengthen, not to duplicate, the outstanding work that is already taking place across Loudoun County. The hub provides consistent division-wide infrastructure that helps

connect identified student needs with available resources, which is really important and exciting, making it easier for our schools and our community partners to really work together, helping to ensure that support reaches the right students at the right time.

So this data on the screen illustrates the significant and ongoing needs across Loudoun and reinforces why a coordinated division-wide system of support is essential for our students and our families. The most recent ALICE data, which stands for Asset Limited, Income Constrained, and Employed, from 2023, shows that a family of four in Loudoun County needs an annual income of approximately $126,000 to meet basic living expenses.

More than 34,000 households, or 24% of Loudoun households, live below the ALICE threshold, with rates approaching 40% in some communities. Within LCPS, 24.7% of our students are considered economically disadvantaged, and that equates out to about 19,000 individual students. Our family liaisons provide approximately 5,000 instances of support for our

students every month. These needs are also reflected in the support provided through Loudoun Education Foundation. So I will now turn it over to Danielle to share more about LEF's phenomenal impact. Thanks, Sarah. Danielle Nadler, Loudoun Education Foundation, and one of our in-house programs. So much of our support, as you all know, we raise funds, we go after grants, and then LCPS is actually providing that service. But Fueled is one of our programs that we have staff, and we provide direct

service. We currently serve 64 school sites, and that's about approximately 7,000 families, and the support includes 300,000 food items. These are stats from last school year. 36,000 snacks, 2,000 pounds of fresh produce, thanks to our growing partner in Middleburg, and 5,000 hygiene products. Together, these numbers demonstrate the scale of the need and the importance of building a coordinated, sustainable system of support.

So behind each of these numbers is a student or a family navigating a challenge that can affect a child's ability to come to school ready to learn. Each month, our family liaisons across our schools support approximately 5,000 students and about 3,100 families with various needs such as food, clothing, school supplies, housing, utilities, healthcare, and connections to community services. Across LCPS, our 98 both full-time and part-time family

liaisons serve as trusted connections between our schools, families, and the community. They listen without judgment, help families navigate complex systems, and ensure they do not have to face difficult circumstances alone. Over this past school year, our family liaisons logged more than 71,000 hours of support for our students and families. Much of this time was spent navigating resources and connecting with community partners to find solutions for family basic needs.

But these hours also represent far more than just transactions. They are moments when a family received help, a student gained access to something essential, and a barrier to attendance, engagement, or learning was reduced. Our family liaisons make this work deeply personal, but the scale of the need needs a coordinated system in order to support them. LEF's Fuel program has established a strong foundation for addressing food

insecurity across LCPS. We're really a leader in this space. There's smaller groups that provide meal bags and snacks, and we're so thankful for them. Often, a church might serve three schools. LEF's Fuel program serves more than 60, and we really are a leader in this space. We communicate with them regularly to ensure there's not duplicated services and to ensure that all 100 schools are served by a student food provider.

LEF's Fuel program has established a strong foundation through weekend meal bags, in-school pantries, break boxes, which are meal kits over long school breaks, and other resources. We're really helping thousands of students and families each week, and the resource hub way to build upon the successful infrastructure and broaden our coordinated response.

So one of the things that we really wanted to do was to gather data and information about how we're supporting currently. So the development of the FACE Resource Hub really began with listening. We gathered input from staff who work most closely with students and families every day, including our family liaisons, school social workers, the McKinney-Vento team, and the school counseling coordinators. And as you can see in this illustration, what we heard was remarkably consistent.

Across roles and schools, staff identified many of the same recurring needs, including food assistance, school supplies, clothing and shoes, hygiene items, transportation and housing support, and connections to health-related resources. So what this illustration also shows is the breadth of the needs that our schools are helping students and families navigate every day. So while the specific need may look different from one student or school to

another, the feedback reinforced the need for a more coordinated and consistent way to respond. And these identified needs became an important foundation for the proposed FACE Resource Hub and really helped shape the model we are sharing with you this afternoon. So one of the most important things to understand is that this initiative, this project, is not about creating new services.

Our schools and community partners are already doing extraordinary work every day to support students and families. The challenge is that those efforts often depend on individual school processes, local partnerships, or available resources. So as a result, students and families may have different experiences accessing support across the division. So the FACE Resource Hub would really give us an opportunity to build the infrastructure that connects those existing efforts

through one coordinated, equitable, and division-wide system. It doesn't replace the great work that is already happening. It strengthens it. So as Renee already mentioned, we really wanted to make sure that the FACE Resource Hub was not developed in isolation. So it is a deliberate result of a planning process designed to ensure that the model reflects both research and the realities within our school and our community.

We began by gathering feedback from staff members who work most closely with our students and families every day, including our family liaisons, McKinney-Vento, school social workers, to better understand the needs that they see across the division. We complemented that work with site visits and research into successful resource hub models that exist around our region to identify effective practices and lessons learned. Using those findings, we developed a comprehensive project

charter that incorporated stakeholder feedback and the expertise of community partners, including our friends at LEF. We then presented the concept to cabinet to refine the vision and ensure alignment with division priorities. And finally, we have planned to convene a cross-departmental workgroup to help guide our planning, implementation, and our long-term sustainability. Each of these steps has helped us to shape a model that builds on existing strengths, reflects stakeholder input, and provides the infrastructure needed to

support our students and families through a coordinated division-wide system. So the goals of the FACE Resource Hub are centered on access, coordination, and student success. Our first goal is about accessibility to essential resources. So we want to ensure that our students and families across LCPS have timely access to the food items that they would need, clothing, hygiene products, things like

that. Our goal two would be to build a coordinated community support system. And what we've learned through our Interfaith luncheon, that we had our first annual Interfaith, is we really, from our community partners in that, is that it would be helpful to have a coordinated community support system in place to strengthen collaboration within LCPS, LEF, our businesses, nonprofits, and faith-based partners.

Our goal three is to reduce barriers to student success. It's such an important one that we're incredibly passionate about because reducing those barriers to success will help with attendance, engagement, and academic success by connecting our kids with essential resources and community supports that they need and deserve. And our fourth goal is to strengthen family engagement and connections, and we

would do that with increasing families' access to school and community resources while also strengthening those relationships between families and schools and community partners. Together, these goals will help us move from individual responses to a more consistent, equitable, and coordinated division-wide system. So our goals define what we hope to accomplish. But the question is: how do we get there?

And these six strategic priorities provide the roadmap for implementation and long-term success. Together, they strengthen the entire system of support for students and families by coordinating resources, streamlining operations, leveraging community partnerships, and expanding equitable access. And the result is a sustainable infrastructure that enables LCPS to respond more efficiently today while building capacity for the future.

And most importantly, this approach allows us to maximize existing partnerships, reduce duplication of efforts, and create new opportunities for family engagement, volunteerism, and student learning. Based on all of our research, our stakeholder feedback, and site visits to established resource hubs, we thought it was really important to select a

closed-loop operational model because it is efficient, effective, responsive, and accountable. This process is intentionally simple. Our schools will submit requests based on identified student and family needs. The hub will then fulfill and deliver these resources directly to the schools. Our school staff will then provide feedback to confirm that their need was met and has made an impact on their students. The items that schools could request might include things like clothing, school

supplies, shoes, hygiene items, and winter apparel. This operational model allows us to track requests, inventory, response times, fulfillment times, recurring needs, and outcomes, creating a coordinated data-informed system that consistently and continuously improves support for our students and our families. So co-location strengthens this partnership, and it's something we were very

excited about from the very beginning of this project. One of the greatest strengths of the model is the opportunity for the FACE Resource Hub and the Loudoun Education Foundation to work side by side while maintaining our distinct roles and responsibilities. The FACE Resource Hub will coordinate school-based referrals and fulfillment and delivery, as you've heard about in previous slides, and outcome tracking, while LEF would continue to lead its outstanding and amazing work in fundraising,

donor engagement, and the Fuel program. By co-locating our operations, we can leverage that shared space, volunteers, logistics, infrastructure to improve coordination, maximize our resources, and better serve students and families. And most importantly, this partnership builds on the strengths of both organizations, creating a more connected and sustainable system of support without changing the unique mission of either organization.

While I've shared this LCPS perspective, I'd love to invite Danielle to share what this partnership means for, um, LEF. Certainly, and I didn't write notes for this, so I'll just- ... talk off the cuff. Currently, LES Fuel program operates out of a warehouse in Leesburg, um, the back of a Walgreens, and it works. It's kind of a makeshift warehouse, but our lease ends December 2027. Not sure if they're flattening it or remodeling it, but for whatever

reason, there's no more space for us. And it's gone well. But as we were chatting about timeline, the frequency in which our teams work together, it's constant. And LES Fuel program, right now, the family liaisons can request and order food via an app. We have a smooth system. But when it's needs outside of Fuel's purview, outside of that pantry meal bag, we

make sure to pass on the request. And of course, you all are getting your requests from your family liaisons as well. So just the idea of being in one shared space. Again, as Renee said, we would still continue fundraising on our own. We have two staff members that we would continue to pay for. But that collaboration, that, um, conversation of, "Hey, we've got requests for school supplies." "Us too. Let's come up with a game plan together." There's a lot of potential there for not duplicating services.

And so one of the really exciting things about the FACE Resource Hub is the aspect of this model having the opportunity to leverage both the strengths within LCPS and the generosity of our broader community, and volunteer opportunities that will emerge out of this partnership and this new resource hub. Our students will be able to participate through work-based learning and service learning experiences, while our businesses and nonprofit organizations such as our faith-based community, volunteers, and donors each have meaningful ways that they

can contribute to the resource hub. Together, this community-supported model expands our capacity, strengthens our existing partnerships, and creates shared ownership of student and family success. Okay, so we are presenting two options for consideration, with the primary distinction being the level of school-based support each model provides.

So both options include a coordinator who would oversee hub operations and build relationships with nonprofits and business partners to coordinate those donations, resources, and funding opportunities. A program assistant that would provide the day-to-day administrative and logistic support for the hub. And our current part-time financial analyst would move to full-time to manage grants funding and purchasing and the financial operations that would be associated with the hub.

Our option one is recommended. This recommended approach, the distinction is we have three specialists associated with this, and each specialist would serve approximately 33 to 34 schools. Okay? Allowing them to build strong relationships with the school teams and develop a clear understanding of the needs within their assigned region, so they would each have a region with about 33 or 34 schools in it.

They would conduct school needs assessments, help coordinate and distribute resources, and serve as each school's primary liaison to the hub. Okay? The regional structure keeps the work closely connected to the schools and supports more timely and consistent responses and strengthens coordination across the division. And for planning purposes, we've also provided estimated costs projected through FY32 so the board can see the anticipated longer-term investment

associated with this model. Now, these projections do not include the transportation support for delivering resources to schools, as that support is already incorporated into the staffing standards for our facilities team. The remaining positions, and I've talked about those, the program assistant. So this one, I just want to point everyone's attention. The key distinction for this one is there are three specialists that would be

regionally responsible for 33 to 34. So when we move to option two, you will see that distinction. So for option two, the overall structure remains the same, but the key difference is the number of regional specialists. This option would have two specialists rather than three, and those specialists would support 50 schools as opposed to the 33 or 34. They would have the same core responsibilities in terms of conducting needs

assessments with the schools, coordinating and supporting the distribution of resources, and serving as the primary hub liaison for the school's aid support. While this option reduces the overall staffing cost, the larger number of schools assigned to each specialist would mean less capacity for individualized school support, relationship building, site visits, and ongoing needs assessment. That difference in capacity is one of the primary reasons that we are really

looking at option one as our recommended. As with option one, we have our projected cost all the way through FY32 to provide a longer-term view of investment, and the transportation would be the same that is incorporated into the facilities team staffing standard. And the reason we're distributing to the schools is, as we've shared in our earlier part of our presentation, transportation is a barrier to our families. So we want to make sure we're shipping to the schools.

Ultimately, both of these options provide the infrastructure necessary to operate the hub. The distinction for consideration is the level of school-based capacity that we're able to provide across the division. Okay. And the proposed timeline here reflects a deliberate phased approach to building a FACE Resource Hub. We begin by establishing a strong foundation through planning

partnerships, staffing, operational systems before launching services and expanding support across the division. As the hub matures, our focus shifts to strengthening partnerships, expanding family engagement, and using the data to drive continuous improvement and building a sustainable model that can grow alongside the evolving needs of our students and families. By moving thoughtfully through each phase, we can really take some time to evaluate

our progress, learn from the data, see where we have trends and needs, which we have hunches, obviously, from our current work. But the hub will allow us to ensure that it is a lasting resource that strengthens our schools and our partnerships and our community. Ultimately, the FACE Resource Hub really is more than a place where resources are stored. It's a place where partnerships are activated, barriers are

reduced, and our community comes together to ensure that every student and every family has the support that they need to succeed. And with that, we are open to questions. Well, it's hard to see a downside here from my perspective. I want to thank you so much, and I thank Dr. Spence for putting this on my radar months ago, sort of just in beginning

conversations. I'm very grateful to be at the table with LEF and sort of following their journey in terms of their needs and obviously the work. I think it goes without saying, but I will say it anyway. The work that your team with FACE and the family liaisons and the Interfaith Lunch and all the things that your small but mighty team does do not go unnoticed, and I know you're working overtime to meet the needs. To me, this just makes sense. When I'm not wearing my school board hat, I help run a ministry through a

nonprofit, and so I know the struggles of working smarter, not harder. Also coming from a Title I background, we know that our family liaisons spend most of their time meeting individual niche needs. And so one thing I want to also point out that I think will be a plus is the opportunity, the cost that you're going to save for the family liaisons to do work

of engaging families in how to get engaged in their school, how to set up a conference, how to know what to do with reading to your child at night, how to get on your high school sports team. All the millions of things that are logistically part of a school life that sometimes get dropped because we just need to meet basic needs so that kids can learn. And so for me, when I came on the board, those were some of the preliminary conversations we were having, even about how can we leverage technology to try and meet some of these needs.

So I'm more than a million percent supportive of moving in this direction. I'm excited to have it come through our committee and hopefully move it to action to the full board. I do have A question. In terms of your regional specialists, I know you said your preliminary, obviously you want option one, and I think having 50 schools

per person would be insane, personally. But having three, 33 schools is a lot. Would you consider looking at the needs and think, we have high density areas of need, I know for sure in Sterling and Leesburg, where I represent. So would you be open to some people having more schools or less schools based on how that ebb and flow works with resources? Absolutely. One of the things that we wanted to do in the presentation was just to give an overview, so that you could see,

we know and recognize, and we go through all of our data, these are the schools that we know have more need. And so we would absolutely be open to making sure that we use that data to adjust the way that our specialists are supporting and who they're supporting based on need. Thank you. And just based off of that, I'm going to give an ask for you as well to get me the numbers for what it would take for five. Okay.

Just to work our numbers down. I know that in these spaces-- Sure. Add seven, sure. Let's start with five. Let's start with five and see if we can get that down a little bit. I know in these spaces, the work is hard. It's taxing, not only on the physical in terms of the delivery and the sorting of supplies, and there's physical work that goes into this.

But there's also the mental load of making sure that people have what they need emotionally to make sure that they are supported when you know that those physical needs exist. And so sometimes we start out at a deficit, and then people get burned out. And so let's just look at what it would take to do more. I would appreciate that. So I will pass the mic to my colleague, Ms. Donahue, and I'm just really appreciative and very, very excited to see where this goes.

Thank you, Chair Chernov. Thank you, Ms. Dawson, Ms. Boyce, and Ms. Nadler, for the excellent presentation. I love talking about how we're going to reduce barriers to student success. I'm thrilled to hear about these ideas. I do have a couple of questions, and they are coming from a place of me not being very good at envisioning non-tangible things.

So when you were talking about this FACE Hub, I was having a hard time telling, are you talking about a physical building or multiple physical locations or systems or all of the above? Because you mentioned infrastructure. I was hoping that you could explain a little more what you are envisioning. That's actually a great question, and we are talking about a physical building that

could store all of our materials, supplies, resources. Many of our schools are trying to find spots in the gym, on the stage, in different areas to sort. So this would be a centralized hub, a location, a physical location where for LEF Fuel program, our need is 2,000 square feet of warehouse space, and then I can't remember the

total amount that you were thinking for your team, but a loading dock. Amazon for free, by the way, delivers our meal bags every week to the schools. So that's Amazon trucks that come to that warehouse that right now is a deck. It's really a makeshift loading dock, but a real loading dock where they could come and- So this would be like a joint warehouse. Yes. And would there also be office space in the same building?

Yes. We would definitely have office space so that all of our people that would be there would have a spot where they could work, workstations, things like that, because our goal is, and one of the exciting things that we did talk about was incorporating our work-based learning students into this. This is a great opportunity to connect, and then the volunteer programs that we have. So we would have to have the ability to meet, to plan, to organize, to train, and all of those things.

And so would LEF move-- Your offices are currently here in admin. Would your offices also move to this new space? In this proposal, it would only be our Fuel team, which is two co-coordinators. We definitely see the value of our Fuel team working closely with some of the FACE team, but we also, as you know, see the value of our three other team members working alongside the teaching and learning team on the fifth floor. So do you have a sense now of,

are you going to be looking for the schools to build a facility or are you going to be looking to buy a building, rent a building, rehab? Yeah. Likely be looking for leased space. Okay. The team has done some preliminary inquiries in looking at the facilities team, and have identified some possibilities. But we sort of pumped the brakes on that until we- Sure ... we want to make sure we don't go too far down that road before we've got board- Mm-hmm ... behind us.

That makes sense. So you'd have the office space there, but then your staff would be going out into the community to spend time in the schools. Right. That's what we're talking about. Well, I think it's two parts. So the staff would actually be there because they have to put hygiene kits together. They have to sort, they have to distribute. They have to do all of those things. But I think the specialists, it's important for them to be in the schools having conversations. What are your specific needs?

What are the times of year that you have bigger needs? We know that at the beginning of school, many of our schools have these needs. So they would be doing basically inventories and having strong connections with the schools that they support, coming back to the hub, getting all of those materials together, and then making sure we distribute it out to the schools. Okay. I think Ms. Chernov was alluding to the same thing that I'm trying to get at with

my next question, because I had written down, do you have numbers on where the need is originating from? As Ms. Chernov was saying, yes, we have 100 schools. It would not surprise me to hear that there are certain needs that you all meet coming from every school, but I imagine the need is higher in some schools, and I'm wondering if you have that information by, is it by geographic area? Is it by grade level? Where are you seeing the greatest pockets of need?

Yeah, that's a great question, and I think the short answer is there's need everywhere, as you alluded to, but there are certainly higher pockets of more concentrated need. Geographically is really probably the best indicator to be able to see that. If you take a look at our numbers of, and percentages of economically disadvantaged families, those are a little bit more concentrated in certain neighborhoods within the school division. However, I will say that I think one of the exciting things about this FACE resource hub is that we do have needs everywhere.

And so while sometimes we're really focusing our efforts on specific pockets or populations, we know that there are still families and students in every single one of our schools who are experiencing barriers and may have a need. And so the resource hub would allow us a centralized area to make sure that the needs are being met no matter where the school is. And so we can ensure that we're really sharing the benefit of these donations or the items, based on where the needs are the

greatest. That absolutely makes sense. If there's a way to provide us with some numbers, some concrete information about where you are putting the most resources without jeopardizing any student privacy or family confidentiality, I think that would be helpful, at least for me. If you're asking us to decide on approving a model that involves two specialists versus three specialists, I think having that information might be helpful.

Okay. Hmm? Or five. Or five or eight, or however many we're going to be asked to approve. But that would be helpful. And then, the other question I had was about physical and mental health services. I feel like I heard a mention of that somewhere in the presentation, but is that something that you anticipate helping the community with finding referrals if you're in need of referrals for mental or physical health services?

So one of the things that we have talked about is how we can provide resources to be sent out to our families. So every student or family that receives something from us will have a list of information and referrals. That's where we have this great opportunity ... kind of synthesize our partnership with some of these organizations, so they will get some information about, "Here's where you can go for this, here's where you can go for that." So we will be able to provide that to our families.

But in terms of us providing that, it would probably be through referral-based. I did not anticipate at this point that we're actually providing the medical care yourselves, but I'm glad to hear that that is something that families could seek out through you as well. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Donahue. While you were talking, I had one more question. Do you anticipate that the space would be able to house parent meetings, events,

things where people could come in and have a central-- I know Head Start does their orientation night and their family nights, and they have people coming in, but while they're there, they're getting backpacks and books and things like that. Is that something you envision as well, or is it purely just warehouse storage? So that actually, I love that question because part of our plan, we have projected out a five-year plan of where we'd like to see it. And when we get to that third year is when we want to start offering the parent

classes and things like that. And in our conceptual thinking of what this place could be, that's why we don't want to have fixed furniture so that we can move things out of the way in case we want to have chairs and we can have parents come in and do trainings and things like that. That's where we can engage our partners to come in and offer some of those classes for them, whether it's something on finances or planning or a part of our family academy that we already have in place.

So that is in our five-year plan should this move along. I appreciate that. All right. I think that wraps up our comments and questions, and thank you so much for being here. This is very exciting. We will move this item to action at our next Specialized Programs & Centers meeting to get it to the full board for approval, and then we will see where it goes. Thank you so much.

All right. We are going to now move on to item 4.02, and we have a presentation today on special programs. And we just have a quick update on elementary school special programs and also admissions windows for our other special programs, and presenting is Ms. Katie Clark. Director of Academic Programs, and I will let you take the floor.

Good afternoon. Today, I'll be providing an update regarding our special programs with a particular focus on elementary school, exploring some potential options, and detailing admissions window for the upcoming 26-27 cycle. So to frame our discussion this afternoon, we'll begin with School Board Policy

5115, which defines special programs and academies as district-approved offerings that provide specialized learning experiences beyond the standard curriculum. These programs are designed to support specific student interests, talents, and instructional goals while expanding educational opportunities for our students. Currently at the elementary level, we have our Spanish Dual Language

Immersion program. We do have some school-based initiatives, such as project-based learning and our charter school models that integrate arts into the instruction. This afternoon, I'll share some community feedback, review regional approaches, and discuss potential future opportunities that could expand specialized learning experiences for our elementary students.

So as we consider future program development, it is always important to understand the interests and priorities of our families. Results from the 2022 community survey demonstrated strong interest in several specialized elementary program options. As you can see displayed here, the highest levels of interest were our Dual Language Immersion at 56%, World Language Academies at 54%, and Fine Arts

Academies at 43%. These findings provided valuable insight into the types of programs families would like LCPS to explore. Since this initial survey in 2022, we have started and have a successful Dual Language Immersion program at two of our schools, and as you know, we're currently getting ready to open our third this school year at Leesburg Elementary. Last fall, we conducted a follow-up survey to reassess community interest and

identify emerging priorities. As you can see here, this is the provided updated feedback from families and other important data points as we evaluate potential future elementary programming opportunities. So of the families that responded, each of them had a little bit different response rate because parents could choose within these options.
